meta.name: Refractory Anaphylaxis — Bee Sting, Biphasic Deterioration, Repeat Epinephrine and Difficult Airway

patient.name: Tyler Brandt
patient.chiefComplaint: Stung by a bee on the left forearm about 6 minutes ago while pulling weeds; now itching all over, breaking out in hives, and says his throat feels like it is 'closing up.'

history.hpi: 19-year-old male, previously healthy college student home for the summer, was pulling weeds along a hedge line in the backyard when he was stung on the left forearm by a bee. Within 3–4 minutes he began itching intensely at the sting site, then over the neck, chest, and both arms. Raised, blanching wheals appeared rapidly. He reports his throat feels 'tight, like it's closing up' and that it is getting harder to pull air in. He is anxious, restless, and repeatedly scratching at his neck. He has a documented severe reaction to a wasp sting two summers ago that was treated in an emergency department; he was discharged with an epinephrine auto-injector and told to carry it. The auto-injector is on the patio table, unused — his mother retrieved it but was afraid to give it and called 911 instead. No known food or drug allergies. Never intubated. No asthma, though he 'sometimes wheezes with a bad cold.' The stinger is still visible in the left forearm.
pastMedical: Severe systemic reaction to a wasp sting 2 years ago — treated in the ED, discharged with an epinephrine auto-injector and allergy referral
Otherwise healthy; no asthma, no cardiac history, no prior intubation
medications: Epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg (prescribed, carried, NOT yet administered)
allergies: Stinging insects — bees/wasps (systemic reaction, ED visit 2 years ago)
history.lastOralIntake: Sandwich and iced tea about 2 hours ago
history.events: Pulling weeds along a hedge in the backyard; stung on the left forearm by a bee roughly 6 minutes before EMS arrival. Itching and hives began within 3–4 minutes and spread to the neck and chest, followed by throat tightness and increasing work of breathing. Prescribed epinephrine auto-injector was retrieved by his mother but never given. No trauma, no fall, no loss of consciousness.

scene.dispatch: Dispatch: 19-year-old male, possible allergic reaction after an insect sting at a private residence. Caller reports he is breaking out in a rash and says his throat feels funny. Conscious and breathing. ALS response.
scene.location: Backyard patio of a single-family home. Patient seated in a metal patio chair beside a garden bed; hedge line and shed at the back of the yard. Warm, sunny afternoon.
scene.time: Saturday, 14:35, mid-afternoon in mid-July, 86°F and sunny
scene.safety: Scene generally safe, but there is visible bee activity around a nest in the hedge 15 feet from the patient. Move the patient away from the hedge before beginning care; do not attempt to capture or kill the insect. Gate to the backyard is narrow — plan the stretcher route early.
scene.bystanders: Mother is the primary historian and is frantic. She confirms the sting was about 6 minutes ago, the ED visit two summers ago, and that the prescribed epinephrine auto-injector is on the patio table — she retrieved it but was 'too scared' to use it and called 911 instead. She has his allergy paperwork from the previous ED visit.
visualCues: Young man sitting upright in a patio chair, leaning forward, visibly anxious and restless
Raised, blanching wheals (urticaria) across the neck, upper chest, and both forearms; he is scratching at his neck
Stinger still embedded in the left forearm with a small venom sac attached and surrounding local erythema
Unused epinephrine auto-injector lying on the patio table next to a glass of iced tea
Gardening gloves and a hand trowel on the ground where he dropped them
Audible bee activity at a nest in the hedge line about 15 feet away
Voice sounds normal on first contact — no hoarseness yet — but he repeatedly clears his throat and touches his neck

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: EMS finds a 19-year-old male roughly 6 minutes after a bee sting. He has urticaria over the neck, chest, and arms (skin/mucosal involvement) AND respiratory compromise — subjective throat tightness with mild bilateral expiratory wheeze and RR 24. That is two organ systems after exposure to a likely allergen, which meets the MATC definition of ANAPHYLAXIS, not a simple allergic reaction. Blood pressure is still normal and there is no stridor yet, which is exactly the trap: crews who wait for hypotension or stridor before giving epinephrine are waiting too long. The protocol threshold is the two-system rule, not the blood pressure. The stinger is still embedded in the left forearm and is still delivering venom. The prescribed auto-injector on the table has never been used. Teaching points for this phase: recognize anaphylaxis by criteria, give IM epinephrine as first-line therapy without delay, remove the stinger without squeezing the venom sac, oxygenate to 94–98%, and treat the wheeze — with antihistamines understood as adjuncts and never as a substitute for epinephrine.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent — speaking in full sentences. No hoarseness, no stridor, no drooling. Oropharynx inspected: mild posterior pharyngeal erythema, tongue and uvula NOT swollen at this time.
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 24, slightly increased work of breathing; mild expiratory wheeze bilaterally in the bases; good air movement, no stridor
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Strong, rapid radial pulse; skin warm and flushed; cap refill 2 sec; no JVD

skin.color: flushed with raised, blanching wheals over neck, upper chest, and both forearms

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Symmetric and intact; restless, scratching at neck
otherFindings: TWO organ systems involved — skin (urticaria) + respiratory (throat tightness, wheeze) = ANAPHYLAXIS by MATC criteria
Normal BP does NOT rule out anaphylaxis — hypotension is a separate, sufficient criterion, not a required one
Stinger with venom sac still embedded in left forearm — continues to envenomate until removed
Prescribed epinephrine auto-injector present on the patio table, never administered
Prior systemic reaction to a wasp sting 2 years ago — high-risk history
No stridor and no angioedema YET — this patient is early, not mild
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: It's getting really itchy… and my throat feels like it's closing up. I got stung two summers ago and it was bad. Am I gonna be okay?

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize anaphylaxis — skin (urticaria) + respiratory compromise = 2 systems
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Assessment 4a-iii — two or more organ systems occurring rapidly after exposure to a likely allergen defines anaphylaxis. Skin + respiratory qualifies here. The crew must NOT wait for hypotension or stridor; a normal BP does not downgrade this to a simple allergic reaction.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for presence of signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis – More severe and is characterized by an acute onset involving: The skin (urticaria) and/or mucosa with either respiratory compromise or decreased BP or signs of end-organ dysfunction OR Hypotension for that patient after exposure to a known allergen OR Two or more of the following occurring rapidly after exposure to a likely allergen: Skin and/or mucosal involvement (urticaria, itchy, swollen tongue/lips); Respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheezing, stridor, hypoxemia); Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea); Hypotension or associated symptoms (syncope, hypotonia, chest tightness, incontinence).

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM anterolateral thigh, 1 mg/mL (adult ≥25 kg — pt 80 kg); vial or auto-injector
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 2 — epinephrine is the PRIMARY treatment for anaphylaxis and the single most time-critical action in this scenario. Adult dose is 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh at the 1 mg/mL concentration. The patient's own prescribed auto-injector on the table is an acceptable delivery route. Time to epinephrine is an explicit patient-safety consideration in this protocol.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Epinephrine administration is the primary treatment for anaphylaxis. If signs of anaphylaxis, administer epinephrine 1 mg/mL at the following dose and route: Adult (25 kg or more) 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh; Pediatric (less than 25 kg) 0.15 mg in the anterolateral thigh; Epinephrine 1 mg/mL may be administered from a vial or via auto-injector, if available. Patient Safety Considerations: Time to epinephrine delivery. Concentration of epinephrine in relation to route.

expectedActions.shortAction: Inspect oropharynx for edema, auscultate for wheeze, assess perfusion — establish a baseline
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Assessment 1–3. This baseline is what makes the later deterioration detectable — the crew must know the tongue/uvula were normal and the lungs only wheezed in order to recognize angioedema and stridor when they appear.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assessment: Evaluate for patent airway and presence of oropharyngeal edema. Auscultate for wheezing and assess level of respiratory effort. Assess for adequacy of perfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Oxygen titrated to SpO2 94–98%; escalate NC → NRB as needed
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 2 — oxygen is a drug with a target range. Titrate to 94–98%, escalating the delivery device as required by the patient's presentation.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen if needed for air hunger or respiratory distress and titrate to a target SPO2 of 94–98%. Depending on patient presentation, this may be accomplished with nasal cannula, nonrebreather, BVM, NIV.

expectedActions.shortAction: Remove embedded stinger without squeezing the venom sac; NO tourniquet, NO ice, NO incision
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Bites and Envenomation Patient Safety 4 and 1 — a retained stinger keeps delivering toxin, so it must come out, but squeezing the sac injects more venom. The protocol explicitly prohibits constricting bands, incision/suction, and cryotherapy, all of which are common student errors on a sting call.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient may still have an imbedded stinger, tooth, nematocyst, or barb which may continue to deliver toxin if left imbedded. Consider safe removal without squeezing the toxin delivery apparatus. Do NOT: Apply tourniquets, tight Ace®/crepe bandage, or constricting bands above or below the site of the envenomation; Incise and/or suction wound to remove toxin; Apply cold packs or immerse the effect extremity in ice water (cryotherapy).

expectedActions.shortAction: Albuterol 2.5–5 mg nebulized for the wheeze (adjunct — does NOT replace IM epinephrine)
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 3 — for respiratory distress with wheezing, consider albuterol 2.5–5 mg nebulized and/or nebulized epinephrine. This is an adjunct to, never a substitute for, the IM epinephrine in action epinephrine-first-dose-im.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If respiratory distress with wheezing is present, consider administering Albuterol 2.5–5 mg nebulized AND/OR Epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL nebulized.

expectedActions.shortAction: IV access — 2 attempts or 90 sec, then IO; cardiac monitor, continuous SpO2 + EtCO2
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Treatment 4 and 8 — establish access with a hard stop at two attempts or 90 seconds before going IO; EtCO2 under 25 mmHg is a marker of poor perfusion. Cardiac monitoring is specifically indicated for patients who go on to receive multiple doses of epinephrine, which this patient will.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 (reading of less than 25 mmHg may be sign of poor perfusion). Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle.

expectedActions.shortAction: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV/IM (80 kg × 1 mg/kg = 80 mg → cap at 50 mg max) for urticaria/pruritus
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 9 — antihistamines treat the urticaria and itching only. They do nothing for airway edema or hypotension. The protocol's Key Consideration 1 is explicit that epinephrine is always first-line; giving Benadryl instead of epinephrine is the classic fatal error this scenario is built to expose.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For urticaria or pruritus, administer a diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg, up to maximum dose of 50 mg IM, IV, or PO. The IV route is preferred for the patient in severe symptoms. As a supplement to diphenhydramine given for urticaria, famotidine, cimetidine) can be given IV in conjunction with diphenhydramine: Famotidine 0.5mg/kg to a max dose of 20mg.

transitions.if: IM Epi given for two-system reaction
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes anaphylaxis on the two-system rule (urticaria + respiratory compromise) and administers epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh without waiting for hypotension or stridor. Stinger is removed, oxygen is applied, and access is established.

Crew anchors on 'hives and itching' and treats this as a simple allergic reaction — gives diphenhydramine and albuterol, withholds epinephrine because the blood pressure is normal and there is no stridor. Untreated anaphylaxis progresses over the next several minutes to airway edema and distributive shock.

phases.name: First Epi given — transient improvement
phases.description: Two to three minutes after IM epinephrine the patient looks better. The wheeze has largely cleared, he is speaking in full sentences again, SpO2 has come up on oxygen, and he says his throat feels 'more open.' He is tremulous, anxious, and palpitating — expected beta-1/beta-2 effects of epinephrine, NOT a new problem. The hives are still there but are no longer spreading. THIS IS THE MOST DANGEROUS PHASE OF THE SCENARIO. A single dose of IM epinephrine has a short duration of effect, the mast-cell mediator release is not finished, and the stinger delivered a full venom load. Crews routinely stand down here — they slow the transport decision, break down the airway kit, and stop reassessing. The protocol's answer to this phase is: transport as soon as possible, keep reassessing, and stay ready to repeat the dose at 5–15 minutes. The crew that packages and moves during this window is the crew that has an airway and a working line when the patient crashes.
phases.triggerCondition: IM epinephrine 0.3 mg was given in the anterolateral thigh. Within 2–3 minutes the wheeze clears, air movement improves, SpO2 rises on oxygen, and the patient subjectively improves — with tremor, anxiety, and palpitations from the epinephrine itself. Symptoms are suppressed, not resolved.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent — full sentences, voice still normal, no stridor. Tongue and uvula remain normal on recheck.
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 20, work of breathing improved; wheeze now minimal and only in the bases; good bilateral air movement
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Strong radial pulse; warm, well perfused; cap refill under 2 sec; fine tremor of the hands

skin.color: still flushed with urticaria over neck and chest, but wheals no longer spreading

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Symmetric and intact; noticeable fine tremor
otherFindings: Improvement is REAL but TEMPORARY — IM epinephrine has a short duration of effect
Tremor, anxiety, palpitations = expected epinephrine side effects, not deterioration
Hives persist — mediator release is ongoing, the reaction is suppressed, not over
Protocol calls for transport as soon as possible with ongoing assessment — do NOT stand down on scene
Second dose of epinephrine may be given as early as 5 minutes after the first if symptoms recur or persist
Cardiac monitoring is indicated because this patient is on track to receive multiple epinephrine doses
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: That shot burned, but I can breathe better. My hands are shaking like crazy and my heart is pounding. Is that supposed to happen?

expectedActions.shortAction: Package and transport NOW — do not stand down during the improvement window
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 10 — transport as soon as possible with ongoing assessment. The transient response to the first dose is not resolution. Every minute spent celebrating the improvement on a backyard patio is a minute of airway equipment and transport capability the crew will not have when the reaction rebounds.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport as soon as possible, and perform ongoing assessment as indicated. Cardiac monitoring is not required, but should be considered for those with known heart problems or who received multiple epinephrine.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess airway, lung sounds, and perfusion q3–5 min — watch for recurrence
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Pertinent Assessment Findings — presence or absence of angioedema, respiratory compromise, circulatory compromise, and RESPONSE TO THERAPY are the tracked findings. MATC Bites and Envenomation Documentation reinforces repeat evaluation because the patient's condition may deteriorate rapidly. Detecting the rebound early is the whole point of this scenario.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pertinent Assessment Findings: Presence or absence of angioedema. Presence or absence of respiratory compromise. Presence or absence of circulatory compromise. Localized or generalized urticaria. Response to therapy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Draw up the second 0.3 mg epinephrine dose now — repeatable at 5–15 min
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 6 — additional IM epinephrine may be repeated every 5–15 minutes if signs of anaphylaxis and hypoperfusion persist. Having it drawn up before the rebound is what makes the 5-minute window achievable rather than aspirational.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If signs of anaphylaxis and hypoperfusion persist following the first dose of epinephrine, additional IM epinephrine can be repeated q5–15 minutes at above noted doses.

expectedActions.shortAction: Cardiac monitor on — patient is on track for multiple epinephrine doses
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 10 — cardiac monitoring should be considered for patients who receive multiple doses of epinephrine. This patient will receive at least two.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport as soon as possible, and perform ongoing assessment as indicated. Cardiac monitoring is not required, but should be considered for those with known heart problems or who received multiple epinephrine.

expectedActions.shortAction: Document dose, concentration, route, and TIME of the first epinephrine
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Key Documentation Elements — the time of administration is what starts the 5–15 minute repeat clock. A crew that cannot say when the first dose went in cannot defend the timing of the second.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: Medications given. Dose and concentration of epinephrine given. Route of epinephrine administration. Time of epinephrine administration. Signs and symptoms of the patient.

transitions.if: Symptoms rebound 6–8 min after first Epi
transitions.condition: Six to eight minutes after the first IM dose the epinephrine effect wanes while mediator release continues. The patient's voice turns hoarse, inspiratory stridor develops, the lips and tongue swell (angioedema), and blood pressure falls into distributive shock. This is a scripted clinical event, not a crew error — it occurs regardless of what the crew does correctly.

phases.name: Refractory anaphylaxis
phases.description: Six to eight minutes after the first dose, the reaction breaks through. The patient's voice is hoarse, he has audible inspiratory stridor, and his lips and tongue are visibly swelling. He is air-hungry and gripping the stretcher rail. Blood pressure has collapsed to 84/50 with a heart rate of 138 — distributive (anaphylactic) shock. SpO2 is 87% despite oxygen and EtCO2 is climbing to 47, signaling ventilatory failure from upper-airway obstruction. This is refractory anaphylaxis, and the protocol has a specific, layered answer for it: a SECOND dose of IM epinephrine (the reaction is not controlled), NEBULIZED epinephrine because stridor is now present, and 20 mL/kg of isotonic fluid because there is hypoperfusion. Simultaneously this is now a predicted difficult airway — angioedema and upper-airway obstruction are named difficult-airway features in the MATC airway protocol — and the crew must be planning escalation with a smaller tube, a bougie, two experienced operators, and a surgical airway available BEFORE they are forced into it. Steroids are NOT the answer here; the protocol says outright there is no proven benefit.
phases.triggerCondition: 6–8 minutes after the first IM epinephrine, the drug effect wanes while mediator release continues. Hoarseness and inspiratory stridor develop, angioedema of the lips and tongue appears, and blood pressure falls to 84/50 with HR 138 — refractory anaphylaxis with distributive shock and impending upper-airway obstruction.

clinicalPresentation.airway: THREATENED — hoarse, muffled voice; audible inspiratory stridor; visible swelling of the lips and tongue; oropharynx now shows a swollen uvula and edematous posterior pharynx
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 32, labored with accessory muscle use and suprasternal retraction; stridor on inspiration; wheeze has returned; air movement decreasing
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Weak, thready radial pulse at 138; cap refill 4 sec; skin now cool and diaphoretic — distributive shock

skin.color: mottled and dusky at the lips despite widespread urticaria

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Symmetric; gripping the rail, agitated and air-hungry
otherFindings: REFRACTORY ANAPHYLAXIS — the reaction has broken through the first epinephrine dose
Stridor is NEW — protocol has a specific answer: nebulized epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL
SBP 84 with cool, diaphoretic skin = hypoperfusion → second IM epi + 20 mL/kg fluid
Angioedema + upper airway obstruction = PREDICTED DIFFICULT AIRWAY per MATC airway protocol
Rising EtCO2 (33 → 47) with falling SpO2 = ventilatory failure, not just hypoxemia
Prep the airway escalation ladder NOW — smaller ETT, bougie, two operators, surgical airway available
Steroids have NO proven benefit here — do not let them displace epinephrine and fluid
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (hoarse, one or two words at a time, stridorous) Can't… breathe. Throat… closing.

expectedActions.shortAction: REPEAT epinephrine 0.3 mg IM, 1 mg/mL (adult ≥25 kg) — anaphylaxis + hypoperfusion persist
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 6 with Treatment 2 — signs of anaphylaxis AND hypoperfusion persist after the first dose, which is the exact trigger for a repeat IM dose. The repeat interval is 5–15 minutes and this patient is 6–8 minutes out. This is the single most time-critical action of the scenario; every other intervention in this phase is built on top of it.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If signs of anaphylaxis and hypoperfusion persist following the first dose of epinephrine, additional IM epinephrine can be repeated q5–15 minutes at above noted doses. Epinephrine administration is the primary treatment for anaphylaxis. If signs of anaphylaxis, administer epinephrine 1 mg/mL at the following dose and route: Adult (25 kg or more) 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh.

expectedActions.shortAction: Nebulized epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL — stridor is now present
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 4 — stridor has its own line in the protocol and its own answer: nebulized epinephrine. This is IN ADDITION to the repeat IM dose, not instead of it; nebulized epinephrine treats the upper-airway edema topically but does nothing for the distributive shock.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If stridor is present, consider administering epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL nebulized.

expectedActions.shortAction: 1600 mL isotonic fluid IV/IO rapidly (80 kg × 20 mL/kg), over 15 min; repeat as needed
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 7 — for signs of hypoperfusion, give 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid rapidly (over 15 minutes) and repeat as needed. At 80 kg that is 1600 mL of normal saline or lactated Ringer's. Anaphylactic shock is distributive — the intravascular space has been dumped into the tissues, and it must be refilled while the epinephrine restores tone.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For signs of hypoperfusion, also administer 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid (normal saline or lactated Ringer's) rapidly (over 15 minutes) via IV or IO, and repeat as needed for ongoing hypoperfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Declare a difficult airway: angioedema + obstruction; stage bougie, smaller ETT, 2 operators, surgical kit open
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Physical Examination 2i–2j — airway obstruction with swelling (angioedema) and upper airway obstruction are explicitly listed as signs of a difficult airway, and Patient Care Goal 5 is to anticipate, identify, and plan for it. In anaphylactic angioedema the airway narrows minute by minute; the window to prepare closes before the window to act does. The plan must be staged BEFORE the crew is forced into it.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Physical Examination – Assess for: Airway obstruction with foreign body or swelling (e.g., angioedema, posterior pharyngeal and laryngeal infections). Signs of a difficult airway (short jaw or limited jaw thrust or mobility, small thyromental space, upper airway obstruction, large tongue, obesity, large tonsils, large neck, craniofacial abnormalities, excessive facial hair, tracheostomy scar or evidence of other neck/facial surgery, trismus). Patient Care Goals: Anticipate, identify, and plan for a potentially difficult airway. Optimize the patient for any advanced airway attempts.

expectedActions.shortAction: High-flow O2; two-person BVM with PEEP 5 cmH2O if ventilation becomes inadequate
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 2 and 4 — escalate oxygen to hold 94–98%, and use BVM in respiratory failure with two-person, two-thumbs-up technique and PEEP. Note the caution: BVM against a swollen glottis moves less air than it appears to, and rising EtCO2 with falling SpO2 signals that ventilation, not just oxygenation, is failing.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation in the setting of respiratory failure or arrest. Whenever possible, the patient's head should be elevated up to 30 degrees. Two-person, two-thumbs-up BVM ventilation is preferred. PEEP should be used with BVM. 5 cmH2O is generally an appropriate initial PEEP setting. Continuous wave-form capnography monitoring should be placed in line.

expectedActions.shortAction: If no line yet: IO after 2 attempts or 90 sec — fluid and drugs cannot wait
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Treatment 8 — the 90-second/two-attempt rule exists precisely for the hypotensive, peripherally shut-down patient. This patient is cool and diaphoretic with a systolic of 84; peripheral veins are collapsing and the crew must not burn five minutes fishing for one.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle.

expectedActions.shortAction: Steroids optional (methylprednisolone 80–125 mg / dexamethasone 8–16 mg) — no proven benefit, never before epi
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 5, read against Key Consideration 7 — the protocol permits steroids but states flatly that there is no proven benefit in the management of allergic reactions and/or anaphylaxis. This action is listed so students see it ranked where the protocol ranks it: an optional adjunct that must never consume time or attention owed to epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine, and fluid.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider Methylprednisolone IV push or IM, 80-125 mg OR Dexamethasone IV push, IM, or PO, 8-16 mg (pediatric 0.5 mg/kg to max of 16 mg). Key Considerations: There is no proven benefit to using steroids in the management of allergic reactions and/or anaphylaxis.

transitions.if: Second IM Epi + neb Epi + fluids given
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes refractory anaphylaxis and delivers the layered response: a second 0.3 mg IM epinephrine dose, nebulized epinephrine 1 mg/mL 5 mL for the stridor, and a 20 mL/kg (1600 mL) isotonic fluid bolus for hypoperfusion, while staging the difficult-airway escalation.

Crew does not repeat the epinephrine — either fixated on the airway equipment, reluctant to redose a tachycardic patient at HR 138, or waiting out the 15-minute end of the repeat window. Upper-airway edema progresses to complete obstruction; the patient becomes hypoxic, bradycardic, and arrests in PEA.

phases.name: Second Epi + fluids given
phases.description: After the second IM dose, nebulized epinephrine, and the 1600 mL bolus, the patient turns the corner — but only partway. Blood pressure comes up to 98/62, SpO2 recovers to 93% on high-flow oxygen, and the stridor softens from loud and continuous to intermittent. The angioedema is still there; the airway is still swollen; the reaction is still live. This phase teaches restraint as much as action. The crew must reassess for a THIRD dose (the repeat interval is q5–15 min, with no fixed cap), but must NOT jump to an epinephrine IV drip: the protocol gates the drip behind cardiovascular collapse persisting despite repeated IM doses AND at least 60 mL/kg of isotonic fluid — which for this 80 kg patient is 4800 mL, and he has had 1600 mL. Antihistamines and steroids can be given now that the time-critical therapy is delivered. The disposition is rapid transport with the airway kit staged, because a patient who needed two doses can need a third en route.
phases.triggerCondition: Second IM epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine for the stridor, and a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus have all been delivered. BP recovers to 98/62, SpO2 to 93% on high-flow oxygen, and stridor becomes intermittent rather than continuous — improved, but the airway is still edematous and the reaction is still active.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Still threatened but improving — voice remains hoarse; stridor now intermittent rather than continuous; lip and tongue swelling persists but is no longer progressing
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 26, still increased work of breathing but with better air movement; wheeze reduced after nebulized epinephrine
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse palpable and stronger at 128; cap refill 3 sec; skin warming after the bolus

skin.color: flushed, urticaria fading at the periphery; lips less dusky

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Symmetric and intact; tremulous from repeat epinephrine
otherFindings: Improved but NOT resolved — the airway is still edematous and the reaction is still active
Third dose remains on the table: repeat interval is q5–15 min with no fixed protocol cap
Epi IV DRIP is NOT yet indicated — it requires collapse persisting despite repeat IM doses AND ≥60 mL/kg fluid (4800 mL for 80 kg); he has had 1600 mL
Antihistamines (diphenhydramine + famotidine) and steroids are now reasonable — the time-critical therapy is already in
Airway kit stays staged and open through transport — the reaction can rebound again
Advance notification: refractory anaphylaxis, two doses of IM epi, angioedema, difficult airway predicted
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (hoarse but full sentences) It's… better. My throat still feels thick. Please don't stop.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess q5 min for a THIRD epinephrine 0.3 mg IM — repeat interval has no fixed cap
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 6 — the protocol authorizes repeat IM epinephrine every 5–15 minutes for as long as anaphylaxis and hypoperfusion persist. It does not stop at two. A patient who required two doses in the first fifteen minutes is a patient who can require a third en route.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If signs of anaphylaxis and hypoperfusion persist following the first dose of epinephrine, additional IM epinephrine can be repeated q5–15 minutes at above noted doses.

expectedActions.shortAction: Hold the epi drip (0.5 mcg/kg/min = 40 mcg/min) — needs collapse + ≥60 mL/kg (4800 mL); only 1600 mL in
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 8 — the IV drip is explicitly gated behind cardiovascular collapse (hypotension with altered mental status, pallor, diaphoresis and/or delayed cap refill) persisting despite REPEATED IM doses IN CONJUNCTION WITH at least 60 mL/kg of isotonic fluid. For an 80 kg patient that is 4800 mL. He has received 1600 mL and his pressure is responding. Recognizing that the gate is NOT open is as much a protocol skill as opening it when it is; the drip rate at 0.5 mcg/kg/min would be 40 mcg/min for this patient if the criteria were later met.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider an epinephrine IV drip (0.5 mcg/kg/minute) when cardiovascular collapse (hypotension with altered mental status, pallor, diaphoresis and/or delayed capillary refill) is present despite repeated IM doses of epinephrine in conjunction with at least 60 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses.

expectedActions.shortAction: Repeat 20 mL/kg (1600 mL) isotonic fluid if hypoperfusion returns; MAP goal 65
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 7 — the 20 mL/kg bolus is repeatable for ongoing hypoperfusion. MATC Shock sets the adult physiologic target at a MAP of 65 mmHg, which gives the crew a number to titrate to rather than a vibe.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For signs of hypoperfusion, also administer 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid (normal saline or lactated Ringer's) rapidly (over 15 minutes) via IV or IO, and repeat as needed for ongoing hypoperfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV (80 kg × 1 mg/kg = 80 mg → cap 50 mg) + famotidine 20 mg IV (80 kg × 0.5 mg/kg = 40 mg → cap 20 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 9 — H1 and H2 blockade for the urticaria and pruritus, with the IV route preferred in the severely symptomatic patient. Correctly sequenced: these come AFTER epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine, and fluid, never before them.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For urticaria or pruritus, administer a diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg, up to maximum dose of 50 mg IM, IV, or PO. The IV route is preferred for the patient in severe symptoms. As a supplement to diphenhydramine given for urticaria, famotidine, cimetidine) can be given IV in conjunction with diphenhydramine: Famotidine 0.5mg/kg to a max dose of 20mg.

expectedActions.shortAction: Keep difficult-airway kit staged en route; least-invasive method that meets the goals
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 1 and Patient Safety 4 — escalate in a stepwise fashion and reserve intubation for when less invasive methods fail to meet the care goals. The patient is oxygenating at 93% and moving air, so he does not need a tube right now — but the swelling means he could in five minutes, and the kit must be within arm's reach when he does.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Generally, the approach is to implement the interventions below in an escalating fashion to meet the patient care goals above. Patient Safety Considerations: Endotracheal intubation should only be used if less invasive methods do not meet patient care goals.

expectedActions.shortAction: Advance notify ED: refractory anaphylaxis, 2 doses IM epi, angioedema, difficult airway predicted
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 10 with MATC Shock Treatment 13 — transport as soon as possible with ongoing assessment, and provide advance notification. The receiving team needs to know this is a two-dose refractory patient with an edematous airway so that airway-capable staff and equipment are at the bedside on arrival, not paged after it.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport as soon as possible, and perform ongoing assessment as indicated. Cardiac monitoring is not required, but should be considered for those with known heart problems or who received multiple epinephrine.

phases.name: Antihistamine only, IM Epi withheld
phases.description: The crew anchored on 'hives and itching,' called it an allergic reaction, and treated it like one — diphenhydramine and albuterol, no epinephrine, because 'his pressure is fine and he's not stridorous.' That reasoning inverts the protocol. Anaphylaxis is defined by TWO organ systems after allergen exposure, and this patient had two on first contact: skin and respiratory. Hypotension is a SUFFICIENT criterion, not a NECESSARY one. Ten minutes later the untreated reaction has done what untreated anaphylaxis does: BP 78/44, HR 134, SpO2 88%, worsening airway edema, cool and mottled skin. The antihistamine did exactly what antihistamines do — it took some of the itch away while the patient decompensated. The rescue is not complicated: give the epinephrine that was owed ten minutes ago, and give it now.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew treated a two-system anaphylactic reaction as a simple allergic reaction — diphenhydramine and albuterol given, epinephrine withheld because blood pressure was normal and stridor was absent. Ten minutes of untreated anaphylaxis have produced airway edema and distributive shock.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Threatened — hoarse voice, early inspiratory stridor, swelling of the lips and tongue now evident
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 30, labored with accessory muscle use; wheeze plus early stridor; air movement decreasing
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Weak, thready pulse at 134; cap refill 4–5 sec; skin cool, mottled at the knees — distributive shock

skin.color: mottled, dusky lips, urticaria still widespread

otherFindings: ANCHORING ERROR — 'hives + wheeze' was anaphylaxis by the two-system rule from first contact
Hypotension is a SUFFICIENT criterion for anaphylaxis, not a REQUIRED one — waiting for it wastes the treatment window
Diphenhydramine treats itch. It does not treat airway edema or distributive shock
EtCO2 has fallen to 28 — approaching the <25 threshold that MATC Shock flags as poor perfusion
Every minute without epinephrine is airway swelling that IM epinephrine may no longer fully reverse
RESCUE: epinephrine 0.3 mg IM NOW, 20 mL/kg fluid, oxygen, nebulized epi for the stridor
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (weak, hoarse) The medicine… didn't help. I can't… get air.

expectedActions.shortAction: RESCUE: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM anterolateral thigh, 1 mg/mL — first-line, owed 10 minutes ago
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Key Consideration 1 and Treatment 2 — when anaphylaxis is suspected, EMS personnel should ALWAYS consider epinephrine as first-line treatment. The protocol's stated patient-safety consideration is time to epinephrine delivery. There is no dose adjustment for having been late; there is only giving it now.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Considerations: When anaphylaxis is suspected, EMS personnel should always consider epinephrine as first-line treatment. Epinephrine administration is the primary treatment for anaphylaxis. If signs of anaphylaxis, administer epinephrine 1 mg/mL at the following dose and route: Adult (25 kg or more) 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh.

expectedActions.shortAction: Name the error: 2 systems = anaphylaxis; one-system rule only applies to a LOCALIZED reaction
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Assessment 4b — a non-anaphylactic allergic reaction involves only ONE organ system (localized angioedema not compromising the airway, or hives alone). This patient had urticaria AND respiratory compromise on arrival, which is by definition anaphylaxis. The debrief must name this misclassification explicitly; it is the root cause of everything downstream in this branch.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-anaphylactic Allergic Reaction: Signs involving only one organ system (e.g., localized angioedema that does not compromise the airway, or not associated with vomiting; hives alone). Key Considerations: Cardiovascular collapse may occur abruptly, without the prior development of skin or respiratory symptoms. Constant monitoring of the patient's airway and breathing is essential.

expectedActions.shortAction: 1600 mL isotonic fluid IV/IO rapidly (80 kg × 20 mL/kg) for hypoperfusion; repeat as needed
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 7 — hypoperfusion is now unmistakable (SBP 78, cap refill 4–5 sec, cool mottled skin). 20 mL/kg rapidly over 15 minutes, repeated as needed for ongoing hypoperfusion.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For signs of hypoperfusion, also administer 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid (normal saline or lactated Ringer's) rapidly (over 15 minutes) via IV or IO, and repeat as needed for ongoing hypoperfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Nebulized epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL for stridor; high-flow O2 to 94–98%
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Anaphylaxis Treatment 4 for the stridor, with MATC Airway Management Treatment 2 for oxygenation targeted to 94–98%. Both are additive to — never substitutes for — the IM epinephrine.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If stridor is present, consider administering epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL nebulized.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport immediately with difficult-airway kit open; anticipate angioedema obstruction
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Patient Care Goal 5 and Physical Examination 2i — anticipate, identify, and plan for a potentially difficult airway; airway obstruction from swelling (angioedema) is a named difficult-airway feature. A late-treated anaphylaxis patient may not fully reverse, and the crew must be ready for the airway they created time for.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Care Goals: Anticipate, recognize, and alleviate respiratory distress. Anticipate, identify, and plan for a potentially difficult airway. Physical Examination – Assess for: Airway obstruction with foreign body or swelling (e.g., angioedema, posterior pharyngeal and laryngeal infections).

phases.name: Second Epi withheld
phases.description: The crew recognized the deterioration but never repeated the epinephrine — fixated on the airway bag, or unwilling to redose a patient already tachycardic at 138, or waiting out the far end of the 5–15 minute window. The airway did not wait. Edema progressed to complete upper-airway obstruction; the patient became silent (no stridor, because no air moves), hypoxic, then bradycardic, and arrested in PEA. This is the scenario's worst outcome and its sharpest lesson: a heart rate of 138 in anaphylaxis is not a contraindication to epinephrine — it is the shock state that epinephrine treats. Resuscitation here is not a standard medical code. This is an arrest of RESPIRATORY etiology, so the airway comes early and passive NRB oxygenation is explicitly not indicated. And the airway that caused the arrest is the same airway that will defeat intubation: when the crew cannot ventilate and cannot intubate through an obstructed glottis, the protocol's answer is a surgical airway.
phases.triggerCondition: The second IM epinephrine dose was never given. Upper-airway edema progressed to complete obstruction; stridor ceased (no air movement), the patient became profoundly hypoxic, then bradycardic, and arrested in pulseless electrical activity.

clinicalPresentation.airway: COMPLETELY OBSTRUCTED — massive angioedema of the tongue, lips, and supraglottic structures. Stridor has STOPPED because no air is moving. BVM produces no chest rise and no EtCO2 waveform.
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic. No spontaneous respiratory effort. BVM attempts meet near-total resistance.
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulseless. Organized electrical activity on the monitor at 32 with no palpable central pulse — PEA.

skin.color: cyanotic — face, lips, and nail beds

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Flaccid, no response to painful stimulus
otherFindings: PEA ARREST from complete upper-airway obstruction — a HYPOXIC, respiratory-etiology arrest
The silence is the finding: stridor stopped because air movement stopped, not because the airway opened
HR 138 was never a contraindication to epinephrine — it WAS the shock epinephrine treats
Respiratory-etiology arrest: manage the airway EARLY; passive NRB ventilation is explicitly NOT indicated
BVM will not move air past an obstructed glottis; ETT will likely not pass the edema
CANNOT VENTILATE + CANNOT INTUBATE → surgical airway is the protocol's answer
IO proximal humerus preferred for adults; epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO early — non-shockable rhythm

expectedActions.shortAction: High-quality compressions: 100–120/min, 2–2.4 in depth, full recoil, minimal interruption
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Consideration 1 — effective chest compressions are the foundational therapy. Rate 100–120, depth at least 2 inches and less than 2.4 inches for adults, complete recoil, minimized interruptions, rotate compressors every 2 minutes.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Effective chest compressions and defibrillation are the most important therapies to the patient in cardiac arrest. Effective chest compressions are defined as: A rate of greater than 100 and less than 120 compressions/minute; Depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) and less than 2.4 inches (6 cm) for adults and children; Allow for complete chest recoil (avoid leaning); Minimize interruptions in compressions; Avoid rescuer fatigue by rotating rescuers at least every 2 minutes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Manage the airway EARLY — respiratory-etiology arrest; passive NRB ventilation NOT indicated
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Special Circumstances 13c — for arrests of respiratory etiology, consider EARLY airway management, and passive ventilation with an NRB is specifically not indicated. This overrides the default adult 'airway is secondary to compressions' posture, because here the airway IS the cause of the arrest and nothing else will fix it.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Special Circumstances in Cardiac Arrest: Arrests of respiratory etiology (including drowning). In addition to the above, consider early management of the patient's airway. Passive ventilation with a NRB is not indicated for these patients.

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO during 1st or 2nd round — prioritize early epi for non-shockable rhythm
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 5 — administer epinephrine during the first or second round of compressions, with explicit instruction to prioritize early administration for non-shockable rhythms. PEA is non-shockable, so the epinephrine goes in early and the crew does not analyze-and-wait.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If feasible, IV or IO access should be obtained. Administer Epinephrine 1mg during the first or second round of compressions. Prioritize early administration of epinephrine for non-shockable rhythms.

expectedActions.shortAction: Cannot ventilate + cannot intubate through the edema → surgical airway
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 11 — when the patient cannot be oxygenated or ventilated by the escalating interventions, or conventional airway approaches are impossible, a surgical airway is a reasonable option where the clinician is competent and the risk of not escalating outweighs the procedural risk. Anaphylactic angioedema producing complete supraglottic obstruction is the textbook case: the BVM will not seal air past the swelling and the tube will not pass it.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: When patients cannot be oxygenated/ventilated effectively using the above interventions, or when conventional airway approaches are impossible, surgical airway management is a reasonable option if the clinician has competency in the procedure and risk of death for not escalating airway management seems to outweigh the risk of a procedural complication.

expectedActions.shortAction: Treat the reversible cause: hypovolemia/distributive collapse — normal saline 2 L IV/IO
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 8d — consider reversible causes; for hypovolemia, add normal saline 2 L IV. Anaphylactic arrest is distributive: the vascular tree is dilated and leaking, and volume plus epinephrine is the only way to fill a circuit that compressions are trying to circulate.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider reversible causes of cardiac arrest which include the following: Hypovolemia. Additions to care include normal saline 2 L IV (or 20 mL/kg, repeated up to 3 times for pediatrics).

expectedActions.shortAction: IO proximal humerus (preferred adult site) if no line; access without stopping compressions
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Consideration 14a-iv and 10 — the proximal humerus is the preferred adult IO site, and access is obtained without interrupting chest compressions.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Additional rescuer obtains IO (or IV) access and gives epinephrine. For IO access: The proximal humerus is the preferred site for adults; The tibial site is preferred for infants and children. IV or IO access without interrupting chest compressions.

expectedActions.shortAction: EtCO2 to gauge compression quality — under 10 mmHg means improve compressions
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Consideration 3 — quantitative waveform capnography monitors compression effectiveness; an EtCO2 below 10 mmHg during resuscitation is a cue to improve compression quality. It also serves as the early indicator of ROSC (a rapid rise of 10–15 mmHg). Note the trap: in a completely obstructed airway, a low EtCO2 may reflect the obstruction rather than the compressions — which is one more argument for the surgical airway.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Quantitative end-tidal capnography (EtCO2) should be used to monitor effectiveness of chest compressions. If EtCO2 less than 10 mmHg during the initial phases of resuscitation, attempt to improve chest compression quality. Is strongly encouraged in patients in cardiac arrest: to monitor quality of CPR; as an early indicator of ROSC (rapid increase of 10–15 in EtCO2); to assist in evaluating prognosis for survival.

expectedActions.shortAction: Resuscitate on scene — compressions in a moving ambulance are less effective and unsafe
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Patient Safety 1–4 and Key Consideration 8 — patients should be resuscitated as close to where they are found as operationally possible; compressions during movement and in a moving vehicle are less effective and hazardous. The instinct to scoop and run with a young arrest patient is strong and must be resisted.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Performing manual chest compressions in a moving vehicle may pose a clinician safety concern. In addition, manual chest compressions during patient movement are less effective in regard to hands on time, depth, recoil and rate. Ideally, patients should be resuscitated as close to the scene as operationally possible. Risks and benefits should be considered before patient movement in cardiac arrest situations.
